name: The Saloon
description: First opened in 1861, The Saloon is one of the oldest running bars in San Francisco. It was originally created by Ferdinand E. Wagner as Wagner’s Beer Hall before being renamed. Wagner lived with his family above the saloon, and his son eventually took over the bar. The Saloon survived the San Francisco earthquake in 1906, slid under the radar through Prohibition by operating under different names, and then was re-established as The Saloon in 1984 under new ownership from Myron Mu. Mu re-cemented The Saloon as a blues, soul, and R&B venue with live music seven nights a week and two different bands per day.
timeline: originally called Wagner's Beer Hall, was eventually renamed as simply the Saloon

name: Ruth Williams Opera House
owner: nonprofit organization Bayview Opera House, Inc.
description: The Ruth Williams Opera House is the oldest theater in San Francisco, originally founded in 1888. In 1968 it became a City of San Francisco landmark, and in 2011 it was put on the National Register of Historic Places. Since its founding, the space has been a community center, site of political protest and activism, and performance space. Today the Opera House’s mission is “to be the Bay Area’s leading provider of Black arts, culture, and artistic skill training.” The Opera House hosts artists in residence, workshops, performances, and offers grants to local artists.
timeline: major renovation in 2014-2016, reopened 2016

name: Golden Gate Bandshell
owner: owned by the City and County of San Francisco and managed by the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department
description: The Golden Gate Bandshell was built in Golden Gate Park in 1900 as a gift to San Francisco from Claus Spreckels. In a speech during the grand opening, he said “My wish is that the pavilion, and the music which will flow forth from it may be incentives to artistic aspirations among all the people of California, and help them to find that happiness, which humanity is to attain in this golden land, in a more abundant degree than in any other under the whole heavens.” In 2020, the bandshell was renovated with new sound and lighting equipment. Today the bandshell offers free concerts every Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday from April through November with over 250,000 attendees annually.

name: Cafe du Nord
owner: Dylan MacNiven alongside his business partner John Larner, with operations managed by Nico Govea
description: In the basement of the historic Swedish American Hall in the Upper Market neighborhood is Cafe Du Nord, a 320 capacity venue. The space started as a bar before becoming a live music venue in the 90s. With over 200 shows a year, the venue has booked several acts before they became big names like Imagine Dragons, Mumford & Sons, Macklemore, OneRepublic, The Lumineers, Brandi Carlile, Phoebe Bridgers, and many more.
timeline: in swedish americna music hall, reopened in 2015 after renovation, 2017 transitioned back to full live music venue

name: Savoy Tivoli
description: The Savoy Tivoli was originally the Savoy Hotel, a coffee house, restaurant, and boarding house popular with Italian immigrants founded in 1907. For 40 cents, patrons could get a full meal, and when meals. In 1967, it was purchased by Fred Kuh and turned into the Savoy Tivoli night club. The club became a symbol of the counterculture, beatnik, and hippie movement with bands like Jefferson Airplane and the Ramones performing. The Ramones 1976 set is credited with helping spark the Bay Area punk movement. In 1987, it was purchased again by longtime patron and fan Claire Kozel who preserved the bar’s history. In the 1990s, noise complaints threatened the Savoy, and their liquor license was removed before efforts by patrons and the mayor helped reopen the bar. The Savoy temporarily closed in 2018 for an earthquake renovation, which was prolonged by the pandemic and passing of Kozel. The bar finally reopened in 2022 under management by Kozel’s son Paul.

name: Swedish American Hall
description: Built in 1907 by the Swedish Society of San Francisco, the Swedish American Hall has hosted Swedish events, community gatherings, church services, weddings, and concerts. The building also houses Cafe Du Nord, a smaller music venue in its basement. In 2015, the Hall began shifting its focus toward live music through a partnership with Noise Pop, an independent San Francisco music and arts festival that had already been booking shows at Cafe Du Nord. While both spaces host performances, the larger Swedish American Hall is better suited for acoustic sets due to its acoustics and sound limitations, according to Noise Pop manager Dawson Ludwig.

name: Grace Cathedral
description: Grace Cathedral is a historic episcopal church with high ceilings and renowned acoustics. Its musical ties started out with the still-running Choir of Men and Boys in the early 20th century before hosting larger jazz and classical shows in the 1960s. Since 2024, there is also a Grace Cathedral Girl’s Choir. Today the venue also hosts immersive sound art installations and artist residencies.

name: 4 Star Theater
description: Opened in 1913 as “La Bonita,” the theater was renamed the “Star” in 1927. In 1946, under new ownership, it was renamed “4 Star.” The venue closed in 1990, but unexpectedly reopened in 1992 under new management of Frank and Lida Lee. The theater gained a reputation as a leading venue for Asian films, and a second screening room was added, expanding its reach. The theater was sold again in 2021 and handed over to CinemaSF who restored it and reopened it in 2022. Now it also hosts live music performances in the main movie screening room along with movie screenings paired with live music. The second screening room was since converted into a record shop.
timeline: originally opened as La Bonita theater, renamed

name: Bill Graham Civic Auditorium
owner: building owned by the City and County of San Francisco, venue managed by Another Planet Entertainment (largest independet concert promoter)
description: Bill Graham began the rock ‘n roll movement in San Francisco in the 1960s. He was a concert promoter for venues around the city including the Fillmore, booking acts like the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane. After his death in 1991, the historic Civic Auditorium venue was renamed to Bill Graham Civic Auditorium. At the same time, the venue suffered significant damage during the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake before its 1991 reopening. The space had previously hosted the DNC in 1920, Martin Luther King in 1956, the Golden State Warriors home court from 1964 to 1956, President Barack Obama in 2007 and 2012 for campaign speeches, and the Dalai lama in 2007. The 8,500 person venue has hosted famous tours including Elvis Presley, the Rolling Stones, Elton John, Prince, Madonna, Oasis, Green Day, Lady Gaga, and many more. It is currently managed by Another Planet Entertainment.
timeline: renamed in 1992 to honor bill graham

name: SF conservatory of music
owner: non-profit educational institution led by President David H. Stul
description: The San Francisco Conservatory of Music (SFCM) was founded in 1917 as the Ada Clement Piano School, before later becoming the San Francisco Conservatory of Music in 1923. The SFCM moved several times, spending 50 years at 1201 Ortega Street before moving to its current Civic Center location at 50 Oak Street in 2006. The Oak Street campus, the Ann Getty Center for Education, has educational and performance spaces to host performances by students, faculty, and visiting artists. In 2021, SFCM further expanded with the nearby Bowes Center for Performing Arts. Notable concert halls include the Caroline H. Hume concert hall with 348 seats and the Barbro Osher Recital Hall with 160 seats.

name: Community Music Center
owner: directed by Executive Director Julie Rulyak Steinberg and was founded by Gertrude Field, nonprofit
description: Community Music Center aims to make music more accessible through low and no cost music lessons and concerts. Originally established as a department of the Dolores Street Girl’s Club settlement house in 1912 by violinist Gertrude Field, it later became an independent organization called Community Music School. Field directed the school until 1946 saying, We are not primarily concerned about the evolution of concert artists, though we give special attention to and encourage those who show exceptional talent. Our aim is to create a musical atmosphere in the home by giving children the means of expression. Hence, ‘how beautiful,’ rather than how well-played or sung, is the comment one hears often in our classes.” In 1953, the organization was renamed to Community Music Center, and in 1983 a second branch opened in the Richmond district. The original Mission District location also went through a significant renovation and expansion in 2024. Today core programs include the Mission District Young Musicians Program where low income middle and high school students in the San Francisco Unified School District have access to music classes, a neighborhood choir for senior citizens and adults with disabilities, and music therapy.

name: The Castro Theater
owner: owned by the Nasser family (specifically the grandchildren of the founding Nasser brothers and Bay Properties, Inc.), who have owned the historic building for generations
description:
The Castro Theater is a historic movie theater in San Francisco’s Castro District, one of the first prominent LGBTQ+ neighborhoods. As the Castro became an increasingly gay neighborhood, the theater evolved with it. KQED rights, “In the outside world, it wasn’t necessarily safe to be openly gay. But inside the Castro Theatre, gay people — mostly gay white men — felt safe to express themselves.” During the AIDS crisis, the theater took on a new role according to queer historian Gerard Koskovich. “It was a place to go after you got done with the two memorial services for people you knew that week,”[...] “You could spend a couple of hours escaping to a movie, or a live show. You could bring people who were sick and they could sit calmly in a safe, secure, comfortable place and know they weren’t going to be excluded if they had signs [of AIDS], like Kaposi’s sarcoma lesions. That people weren’t going to pull away from them. They could remain part of the community that had been built there.”
The theater most commonly showed LGBTQ films, foreign films, arthouse and indie films, and classic movies. 

In 2008, the Castro Theater hosted the world premiere of Milk, a movie about gay rights advocate and SF politician Harvey Milk. 

In 2022, it’s announced that local concert promoter, Another Planet Entertainment, will be leasing and renovating the Castro Theater as a live music venue to open in 2023. This decision split the local community, with many concerned that the venue’s roots in queer cinema history would be lost. A “Save the Castro Theater” campaign was launched, and a prominent concern was over what would happen to the interior of the venue. The venue’s historic movie palace seating was fought over in city hall before being removed during the $41 million renovation. Other people argued that queer music could be just as meaningful as movies and were excited to see the venue preserved. 

The venue was closed for renovations from 2024 through 2026, and celebrated its grand reopening with a screening of The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and a drag show by local performer and Oasis owner, Darcy D’rollinger.

name: The Warfield
owner: owned by A&C Ventures and operated by Goldenvoice (a division of AEG Presents)
description: The Warfield originally opened as Leow’s Warfield, a movie theater named after San Francisco silent film and stage actor David Warfield. In 1979, Bill Graham turned the theater into a live-music venue, where it gained recognition with Bob Dylan’s 14-show residency in 1979, 12-show residency in 1980, and a 15-show Grateful Dead run in 1980. The Jerry Garcia Band was also the unofficial house band through 1995. The floor seats were removed in the 1980s to increase the venue’s capacity and allow more space for dancing. Bill Graham Present’s final show was in 2008, and then the venue was renovated and reopened under Goldenvoice management. Notable acts at The Warfield include U2, Prince, David Bowie, The Clash, Metallica, Guns N’ Roses, and more.

name: Great Star Theater
description: The Great Star Theater originally opened as The Great China Theater, featuring Cantonese opera, before pivoting to showing Chinese and American films during World War II. The venue declined in the late 20th century before being reopened in 2021 as a nonprofit. Today the 500 seat theater once again features Cantonese opera alongside guzheng music, comedy, magic shows, burlesque, and independent film, aiming to “revitalize Chinatown’s artistic legacy.”

name: Bimbo's 365 Club
owner: owned by family of  Agostino "Bimbo" Giuntoli
description: Bimbo’s was named for its founder, Agostino Giuntoli, an Italian immigrant who arrived in San Francisco in the 1920s. His boss couldn’t pronounce his name, and called him bimbo, Italian for “boy,” which became his nickname. Giuntoli originally opened 365 Club, a speakeasy on Market Street in 1931. The same year, nightclub Bal Tabarin opened on Columbus Avenue. In 1951, Giuntoli merged both sites, opening Bimbo’s 365 Club in the former building of Bal Tabarin. He ran the club until his retirement in 1970 when the club mostly closed except for private events. In 1988, Giuntoli’s grandson reopened the club and turned it back into a live concert venue. It’s since hosted Adele, Lara Marling, The Black Angels, and The Flaming Lips.
timeline: originally started as a speakeasy and gambling club on Market Street by Agostino "Bimbo" Giuntoli and Monk Young before moving to its current location on Columbus Avenue in 195

name: Herbst Theater
owner: San Francisco War Memorial and Performing Arts Center, which is a facility managed for the City and County of San Francisco.
description: The Herbst Theater is housed in the War Memorial and Performing Arts Center in the Civic Center. The theater hosts bay area arts organizations including City Arts and Lectures, SFJAZZ, the San Francisco Philharmonic, the African American Shakespeare Company, and more. The venue is also famously the site of the United Nations Charter signing in 1945. The theater got its name in the 1970s when the Herbst Foundation paid for it to be renovated.

name: Dawn Club
description: Originally a Prohibition-era speakeasy, the Dawn Club was central to San Francisco’s jazz revival during the 1930s and 1940s. During World War II, its live radio broadcasts, Air Shots From the Dawn Club, broadcast music on Friday and Saturday nights across the Pacific, featuring music from Lu Watters and his Yerba Buena Jazz Band. Financial troubles forced the club to close in 1946, but it was revived in 2023 with a new iteration of Dawn Club in the same historic building. Today the club features nightly swing and jazz residencies.
timeline: prohibition era speakeasy and jazz club, modern iteration opened 2023

name: Stern Grove Festival
address: Sigmund Stern Grove, located at the corner of 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard
description: Stern Grove Festival is the nation’s longest-running free nonprofit music festival. It takes place in a natural amphitheater surrounded by eucalyptus, redwoods, and fir trees. The Sigmund Stern Recreation Grove was given to San Francisco by Rosalie Meyer Stern in honor of her late husband Sigmund Stern, a civic leader. She intended the site be used as a recreation and concert space and founded the Stern Grove Festival Association nonprofit in 1938. The first season happened that year with 12 concerts. Since beginning, the festival has hosted 1,000+ concerts, 5 million attendees, and raised over 1 million dollars. Stern Grove explains that it takes nearly $6 million each year to produce the festival, with money contributed by donors and sponsors.

name: Presidio Theater
owner: Presidio Theatre is operated as a non-profit performing arts center founded and led by board chair Peggy Haas
description: Originally built in 1939 by the Works Progress Administration, the Presidio Theater hosted entertainment for the military and their families for 60 years. In 1994, the US Army left the Presidio, turning the land over to the National Park Service. The theater was closed for over 20 years until 2017 when it underwent a $44 million renovation by Peggy Haas through the Margaret E. Haas Fund, in partnership with the Presidio Trust. In 2019, the theater opened to the public where it now hosts performing arts shows spanning dance, theater, music, cinema, and private events.
timeline: major renovation. originally a movie theater for soldiers

name: Cow Palace
description: The Cow Palace was originally built for rodeo and livestock events, but hosted many large-scale concerts because there was no other large venue in the 60s. Box office manager Bruce Ede explains, ““There were no other venues for arena tours,” explains Bruce Ede, the Cow Palace’s longtime box office manager. “It was the Cow Palace and the [Oakland] Coliseum, there wasn’t anywhere else.” Notable shows included Elvis Presley, the Beatles, The Who, The Doors, The Grateful Dead, The Rolling Stones, Pink Floyd, Eric Clapton, David Bowie, Elton John, Neil Young, AC/DC, Tom Petty, Michael Jackson, The Police, Van Halen, Prince, Metallica, Fleetwood Mac, U2, Nine Inch Nails and Nirvana. The arena also hosts ice hockey, soccer, basketball, political conventions, and dance shows. Rumors have circled about the building getting sold for housing or data centers, but nothing is official.

name: The Rite Spot Cafe
owner: owned by Jose and Luciana Hu, and managed by their daughter, Christina Hu
description: Hosting sidewalk music every night, The Rite Spot is a neighborhood spot for dinner, drinks, and a show. It’s been family owned and woman owned for over 70 years in the Mission. After decades of hosting music, the Rite Spot finally got an entertainment permit in 2020 after the Entertainment Commission received over 120 letters in support. The family didn’t realize they needed a permit for the music, and had managed to run for so long without one because they had never received a noise complaint. They host diverse music from blues to opera to folk to comedy shows on their sidewalk and indoor stage.

name: The Fillmore
description:
In the historic Fillmore district, The Fillmore has a standing-room only ballroom for 1,000 people. It was started  in 1954 by African American businessman Charles Sullivan who focused on booking Black music and jazz artists like James Brown, Ike & Tina Turner, Louis Armstrong, and Billie Holiday. Promoter Bill Graham began booking shows at The Fillmore in the mid 1960s, and he took over the venue after Sullivan’s unsolved murder in 1966. Graham transformed the venue into the center of the San Francisco psychedelic and counter culture movement, hosting the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Doors, and Santana. The Grateful Dead played 51 shows there between 1965 and 1969. Since 2007, it has been managed by Live Nation, and Live Nation has named other national clubs after The Fillmore. 

The Fillmore is known for its iconic Fillmore posters which began in 1966. The venue commissions a custom poster for each sold-out show, and gives them out to fans for free. A collection of historic posters is in the venue today. There are also free red apples as attendees enter the venue.
timeline: originally Majestic Hall, opened in 1912, renamed Fillmore AUditorium in 1954, Bill Graham began promoting concerts here 1965, Live Nation aquires management in 2007

name: Caffe Trieste
description: Caffe Trieste is a historic coffee shop in North Beach that’s famous for being the first espresso coffee house on the West Coast, opening in 1956. It also became a hub for Beat movement writers in the 50s and 60s, alongside poets, painters, and artists. The coffee shop is also known for its Saturday afternoon concert series, running since the 1970s, and featuring local musicians.

name: The Masonic
owner: the Masons of California (the California Masonic Memorial Temple), while the venue's events, bookings, and operations are managed and operated by Live Nation.
description: The Masonic, officially known as SF Masonic Auditorium, is both the meeting space for the Masons of California’s Annual Communication and a concert venue managed by Live Nation. They host about 80 public events and concerts annually.

name: Peacock Lounge
description:
Peacock Lounge is a historic, Black-owned social space and venue in the Lower Haight. It was never intended to become a nightclub. The lounge was originally started in 1960 when the nonprofit Unity Mutual Benefit Association, incorporated in December 1960, established the space beneath its Masonic hall as a private gathering place for Black Masons and community members.

Since then, the venue has largely hosted private events. It’s not until recently that it’s become more open to the public. A renovation sponsored by a city grant helped renovate the space, and now the Lounge hosts Jazz Fridays which aim to honor San Francisco’s black jazz history and give platforms to Black artists. Manager Jerome Walker said, “We have a lot of Black artists who’ve been looking for a place to perform. You know the whole Fillmore was a place where noted Jazz musicians, known nationally or internationally, would come to play. We are making it more acceptable for the public.”

name: The Stud
owner: a worker-led cooperative called The Stud Collective
description:
The Stud is one of San Francisco’s longest running gay bars, hosting DJs, drag, karaoke, and more since its 1966 opening. It first opened at 1535 Folsom Street before moving to Ninth and Harrison in 1987. After more than 50 years of operation, The Stud’s building owner raised the rent from $3,800 to $9,500, tripling the monthly rent and prompting the owner Michael McElheney to retire and close the bar. The news of the closure sparked activism in the community with a “Save Our Stud” Facebook group that gained traction and organized into a worker-owned collective. Now The Stud is owned by a collective of 18 artists, DJs, nightlife staff, and tech workers, including local drag queen Honey Mahogany. The collective purchased the bar from McElheney in 2016 and now everyone’s an equal owner. According to collective member Nate Albee, The Stud is “the very first co-op nightclub in the United States.” They established codes, committees, and processes to streamline decision making and mitigate internal conflicts among the group. They also got the club secured as Legacy Business status to increase city support and stability. 

The Stud closed in May 2020 amidst the pandemic before reopening in April 2024 at a new location down the street at 1123 Folsom Street. They are also starting a new initiative, Stud School of Drag, a program to mentor aspiring drag performers. Honey Mahogany, one of the co-op members, will run the program. The Stud serves as a case study of unconventional ownership and community support for a music venue.
timeline: originally opened 1966 at 1535 Folsom, closed 2020 in pandemic, reopened in 2024 at new location, run by worker-owned stud collective

name: Audium
description:
Audium is an experimental spatial audio experience. With 176 speakers designed as “sound sculptures,” listeners sit in a dark, 49-seat theater and experience the audio around them. Programming includes artist collaborations and residencies. 

The idea of Audium first began in the 1950s, when co-founder Stan Shaff was exploring how space intersected with live performance. Stan and his cofounder Dough McEachern met while teaching high school students in San Francisco; Stan was exploring spatial audio and Dough was engineering audio systems for live compositions. A series of performances and projects across the city attracted attention to the idea of spatial audio in the following years. 

“Space and sound seem to go especially well together when the sound is produced electronically, but the possibilities of the space-sound continuum have seldom been so extensively explored as they were Thursday night at the San Francisco Museum of Art in a program presented by Stanley Shaff and Douglas McEachern.” 
SAN FRANCISCO CHRONICLE, Oct. 17, 1964 , Space-Sound Continuum in Total Darkness, Alfred Frankenstein, Music Critic

In 1967, the first Audium theater opened with two weekly performances and an initial 44 speakers, but closed in 1970 when the building was sold. In 1975, a new building was opened for Audium performances, where artist residencies and performances have been hosted since and the number of speakers has grown to 176.

name: Palace of Fine Arts Theatre
owner: the Palace of Fine Arts League, a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization
description:
The iconic Palace of Fine Arts was built in the Marina District in 1915 for the Panama-Pacific Exposition to celebrate the completion of the Panama Canal and recovery from the 1906 earthquake. It was a 140,000 square foot event space and complex. Originally just a temporary Roman-inspired structure, the structure was so well loved by the public that it stayed. By the 1950s it was decaying, and rebuilt more permanently from 1964 to 1974. 

In 1970, 1/3rd of the old original event hall was turned into a 1000 seat performance center. The other 2/3rds housed The Exploratorium science center from 1969 to 2013. On October 6th, 1976, the theater hosted the second presidential debate between Gerald Ford and Jimmy Carter. Today the Palace of Fine Arts Theater is still managed by the non-profit Palace of Fine Arts league and hosts concerts, comedy shows, ballet, and community events.

name: Old First Concerts
description: Old First Concerts is a historic music venue inside the Old First Church that has been hosting concerts year-round since 1970. The venue primarily features chamber, classical, and jazz music and the church’s grand piano.

name: Great American Music Hall
description:
Great American Music Hall is a historic San Francisco independent music venue. It opened in 1972 after being a music club under different names since the early 1900s. Through the 70s and 80s, the venue became the home of live album recordings and comedy special tapings. Notably, The Grateful Dead recorded their live album, “One from the Vault” at the hall in 1975. In 1982, Robin Williams filmed his HBO special, “An Evening with Robin Williams” at the venue. The ornate interior of the hall also largely hasn’t changed since its original opening. 

In 2013, it was voted the sixth-best rock club in America in a Rolling Stone reader poll. In 2025, the venue had its most profitable year in decades, accredited to building a reputation with post-pandemic audiences and hosting more shows than ever before. While many indie venues struggle to survive against corporate-backed venues, manager Fred Barnes says, “We have the best room. Some artists specifically want to be here and nowhere else.”

Small venues like GAMH still struggle though, general manager Fred Barnes said at a San Francisco Music Week Industry Summit in 2026, ““This last year we made by far in revenue the most we’ve ever made, but at the same time the costs were unbelievably higher than they’ve ever been before.”
timeline: originally opened 1907, current name opened in 1972

name: The Depot
description: The Depot is an underground, student-run music venue in the basement level of the Cesar Chavez Student Center at San Francisco State University. With events funded by the student body, the venue hosts small concerts, jazz nights, comedy shows, and open mics.
timeline: San Francisco State Univeristy

name: The Plough and Stars
description: Located in Inner Richmond, The Plough and Stars is a historic Irish pub and music venue. They host weekly traditional Irish music and dancing, alongside Americana, roots, and bluegrass nights.

name: The Mabuhay Gardens
description:
The Mabuhay Gardens, known affectionately as The Mab, was a Filipino restaurant, nightclub, and music venue that opened in the early 1970s. In 1976, promoter Dirk Dirksen began booking punk and new wave shows, cementing the venue as central to the city’s punk scene. The Mab also hosted Filipino performers and was closely tied to the local Filipino community. Punk writer V Vale, says of The Mab’s early days, “All the bands, punk bands all over the world wanted to come to San Francisco and play the Mabuhay because that’s the only club there was. No one else would let punk shows happen that I know of, at least. And so that made it very simple. You go to San Fransisco, you play the Mabuhay. You go there every night, there’s a punk show.” 

The Mab closed in 1987, but the venue continued as various entertainment spaces. Nearly four decades after its closure, a group of local investors and nightlife veterans began working in 2025 to revive the Mabuhay Gardens and bring back live music to the space. They launched a Go Fund Me with a $4.5 million goal. The newly revived Mab is not intended to directly recreate the original venue; rather the owners want to create a broader cultural and arts event space to host poetry, neighborhood meetings, live music, yoga, lectures, and more. Co-owner Tom Watson envisions the space as a “a creative platform for anyone who wants to do anything.” 

The revival has generated some skepticism, especially after one of its opening events was for SF Tech Week. There was concern that the reopening was using the original name without maintaining its Filipino, punk ethos. Watson says, “We will never be able to recreate the Mab, and that meant some special things to many people, and we want to build from that sort of open stage and raucous energy."
timeline: originally opned 1976, closed in 1987, being brought back now (2025)

name: Hotel Utah Saloon
owner: Andrea Cochran, Mohamed Bacchus, and Damian Samue
description: Hotel Utah Saloon was originally built in 1908 serving as a bar pre, during, and post prohibition. During prohibition, it’s customers included ““Gamblers, thieves, politicians, hustlers, friends of opium, goldseekers, godseekers, charlatans, police” and “fancy miscreants.” In 1977, it was bought by Paul Gaer who built a stage to turn it into a live music venue and renamed it The Utah. Whoopi Goldberg, Robin Williams, and the Pickle Family Circus were early performers. Today it’s known for Monday Open Mic nights, weeknight matinee shows, and shows spanning comedy, poetry, and music. Now in 2026, the bar is up for sale. The current owners, Andrea Cochran, Mohamed Bacchus and Damian Samuel are looking to retire and sell the bar for $235,000. The bar is attached to the Hotel Utah, which is managed separately. Cochran said to the SFGate, ““I think the fantasy would be to find someone who really values it for its cultural contributions,” Cochran said. “I think it’s pretty well known amongst people in the music scene in the city. And we’d hope that it would remain a live music venue.” [...] “““I would want them to know that we hope to keep it as great as it’s always been, and we’ll really try to find a caring buyer who will be a good person, and not to worry,” she said. “We don’t want people to freak out or something. Hopefully, we’ll find the right person who will love it and carry it on.” If they can’t find a buyer, the Hotel Utah Saloon may have to close.

name: El Rio
description: El Rio is a historic Mission District gay bar, started by couple Malcolm Thornley and Robert Nett in 1978, inspired by their love of motorcycles, leather, and Brazil. It was the first gay bar with queer salsa in San Francisco. Malcolm and Robert owned the bar until 1997 when they retired and it was taken over by Dawn Huston. In 2019, the property was threatened with sale and almost closed before the city purchased the building for $8.6 million through its Small Sites Program. Notable events include Salsa Sundays, a queer latino event that’s been running for over 30 years, and Mango, a monthly daytime tea party for women of color. El Rio hosts activist events, performances, live music, and dancing.

name: The Deluxe
owner: Led by Christian Beaulieu (a former bartender and musician at the club) and Jay Bordeleau
description:
The Deluxe has gone through many variations of the same name since opening in 1978. The venue first opened as a gay bar, the Deluxe Bar. It later became a jazz bar and was renamed Club Deluxe. In 2023, Club Deluxe closed, and it was announced in 2026 that Club Deluxe would come back as The Dluxe under the ownership of longtime patron and former bartender Christian Beaulieu and Jay Bordeleau, founder of nearby bar, Mr. Tipples Jazz Club. The new Deluxe will host live music every night and expand into genres beyond jazz like blues. 

The venue is required to host music every night since it has a Type 90 liquor license which means alcohol can’t be served on days without a ticketed live show.
timeline: 1978–1989: Originally opened as an LGBTQ+ space and gay bar called the Deluxe Bar.1989–2023: Transformed into an intimate, old-school New York-style jazz house known as Club Deluxe.2023–2026: Closed temporarily due to the pandemic and landlord disputes before being restored and resurrected by its new stewards in June 2026

name: Davie's Symphony Hall
owner: the San Francisco War Memorial and Performing Arts Center
description: Home of the San Francisco Symphony, the Louise M. Davies Symphony Hall was completed in 1980. The Symphony previously performed at the War Memorial Opera House alongside the San Francisco Opera House and San Francisco Ballet; by getting its own concert hall, they were able to expand to year-round performances. Today the San Francisco Symphony hosts orchestral series, film screenings with live orchestras, small ensembles, and community events.

name: SF Eagle
description: Iconic gay leather bar, SF Eagle, first opened in 1981 in San Francisco’s SoMa neighborhood. Through the AIDS crisis, the Eagle founded Up Your Alley (Dore Alley) fair as an AIDS benefit and became a hub of grassroots fundraising and memorials. Mayor Art Agnos declares a day in honor of the manager, Terry Thompson, who drove the Eagle’s fundraising. In 1998, the Eagle was sold, with a condition that the name “Eagle” was kept in the name, so the bar became Eagle Tavern. In 2012, it was sold again and renamed back to SF Eagle. The Eagle primarily hosts local underground bands, lip-syncing, drag shows, cabarets, and electronic parties. Since its opening, the Eagle has raised more than $30 million for the community.

name: The Lab
owner: The Lab in San Francisco is operated as a non-profit arts organization and does not have a private "owner," but it is directed by Executive Director Andrew Smith
description: The Lab is a nonprofit experimental arts organization and performance space founded by San Franciscso State University art students in 1984. It’s dedicated to providing support and funding to underrepresented artists, allowing them to create more experimental and risky work. They write that, “The Lab is a catalyst for artistic experimentation.” The venue relocated to its current Mission District space in 1995, where it hosts diverse programming from exhibitions, experimental sound shows, films, poetry, literary arts, concerts, and more. The Lab is also known for its artist residency program, which has hosted Nan Goldin, Barbara Kruger, David Wojnarowicz, Barry McGee, Kim Gordon and Kathleen Hanna.

name: Noe Valley Ministry
description: The historic Noe Valley Ministry was built in 1888, and was one of the few wooden churches to survive the 1906 earthquake. It started as Noe Valley Presbyterian Church in 1881 before becoming Lebanon Presbyterian Church in 1884 until its closing in 1977. In 1984, the church was re-opened as the Noe Valley Ministry and actively supported the AIDS crisis during the 1980s. The Ministry hosted the Noe Valley Music Series from 1981 to 2011, hosting intimate acoustic and jazz shows. Today the church still hosts classical, jazz, and chamber concerts alongside youth performances.

name: DNA Lounge
description:
DNA Lounge is a historic SF dance club featuring all-ages events, dance parties, themed nights, and live music. With two stages, four dance floors, six bars and a restaurant, DNA Lounge has been voted "Best Dance Club" every year since 2008. In 2008, after years of legal battles, the club’s new owner, Jamie Zawinski, secured all-ages operating permits to host events for all ages instead of just 21+. Shortly after though in 2009, The California Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) launched an investigation against the club in 2009 for “running a disorderly house injurious to the public welfare and morals" asking for permanent revocation of the club's alcohol license, which would close the club. Community members were outraged that accusations were with regard to LGTBQ+ events, and believed that this was a retaliation against the all-ages permit. 

In 2009, ABC ruled to revoke DNA Lounge’s alcohol license which DNA appealed, challenging the constitutionality. A legal defense fund was set up with donations. Eventually a settlement was reached and DNA got a 25 day suspension instead. 

In 2011, Zawinski merged with the neighboring pizza shop, creating a join all ages venue and restaurant.
timeline:
Renovated: July 13, 2001
Expanded: October 23, 2012

name: Pier 23 Cafe
description: Pier 23 Cafe is a historic restaurant and bar hosting waterfront live music including a weekly Sunday Blues Jams and local jazz bands.

name: BIX
description: BIX is a combination speakeasy, supper club, and saloon with a two-story dining room and elegant art-deco decor. They host nightly live jazz ranging from solo piano sets to jazz duos and trios.

name: 1015 Folsom
description: Before 1015 Folsom was one of the hottest dance clubs in San Francisco, the building housed, [Sutro Baths], a gay bathhouse in the SOMA neighborhood, from 1977 until 1984. During the height of the AIDS crisis, the bath house was shut down by city officials. The space was then reopened as Das Klub in 1986 by Ira Sandler. He later renamed it to 1015 Folsom. The venue is credited with becoming a “cornerstone of the city’s electronic music scene, hosting a number of legendary house and techno parties throughout the late ’80s and ’90s.” Today the venue spans 20,000 square feet, three floors, and 5 separate rooms. Notable performers include Madonna, Tiësto, Giorgio Moroder, Fatboy Slim, Pabllo Vittar and Dave Chapelle.

name: Adobe Books
description: Founded in 1989, Adobe Books became a community space for artists, musicians, writers, and readers, affectionately known as, “The Living Room of the Mission.” It transformed a back storage room into a gallery in 2001 and also regularly hosts musicians in the shop. In 2012, a rent increase almost forced the store to close before a group of supporters came together to form a cooperative business to save Adobe Books. They raised $60,000 and found a new location in the Mission District where they currently run as an almost entirely volunteer-run independent bookstore.

name: Bottom of the Hill
owner: Ramona Downey, Kathleen Owen, and Lynn Schwarz
description:
Bottom of the Hill was chosen by Rolling Stone magazine in 1999 as "the best place to hear live music in San Francisco.” Affectionately known as Bottom, the venue hosts live music 7 nights a week. It’s repeatedly won the Readers' Poll Best of The Bay award for Rock venue, and is known as the heart of San Francisco’s indie rock scene. The venue has hosted a huge number of now-famous artists when they were still relatively unknown, including Arcade Fire,[1] Avail, Bad Religion,[4] Beastie Boys,[1][3] Black Rebel Motorcycle Club, Blink 182, Bright Eyes, Cake, Cat Power,[3] Death Cab for Cutie,[3] Elliott Smith,[1] Fu Manchu,[4] fun., Green Day, Kid Rock,[1] Lush, Marilyn Manson,[1] Alanis Morissette,[1] Nashville Pussy,[4] Neutral Milk Hotel, Oasis,[1] Queens of the Stone Age,[3] The Donnas,[4][3] The Flaming Lips, The Mighty Mighty Bosstones. 

In January 2026, the owners announced in a facebook post that Bottom of the Hill would be closing at the end of the year. The venue is owned by three women, Ramona Downey, Kathleen Owen, and Lynn Schwarz (the late Dave and Tim Benetti were also original owners). They wrote

 “This legendary business will have lived to the ripe old age of 35, a long stretch in San Francisco for an independent rock ‘n’ roll venue of our size. It has been a wonderful trip, and we are full of stories and memories. We have hosted tens of thousands of musical artists and have been a community partner as well, holding numerous benefits, school recitals, weddings, birthdays, and memorials. Let’s have one more solid year of memories together and bid a fond farewell to a legendary venue.
We will curate one more year of great shows, enticing bands that make up our history to come back for one final play on our stage. Let’s celebrate, for one more spin, how far we came, how many bands we hosted, how many amazing people we worked with. We want to thank the bands, their agents, managers, and roadies, for always bringing the most exciting shows to our intimate room, with the analog board at the helm. And most especially, we wish to thank our loyal customers who kept us in business for this long and told us, in so many ways, that we were doing things right.
As the owners of Bottom of the Hill, we (Ramona Downey, Kathleen Owen, and Lynn Schwarz), are three women in different phases of our lives (and a sad RIP to Tim Benetti, our beloved fourth, whom we recently lost). Part of what has made our partnership so functional and wonderful are the perspectives of three strong women from different generations and backgrounds. We come together on so many issues but also bring our own unique life experiences to this business. Together we have nurtured Bottom of the Hill over the decades—it’s our child. We include in our family the incredible staff who are the ones who keep our business on the map. Several of our team have been with us for well over a decade and some the whole time, making this decision to shutter extra difficult.  
We will miss you all so much after this one last star-studded year. 2026 is our big victory lap! Please come celebrate with us. Not with a whimper, but a bang!”” 

It was announced in late October 2026 though that the venue was being purchased! Ramona, Kathleen, and Lynn originally didn’t want to sell the venue in fear of the spirit of Bottom being lost, but music superfan and regular Michele Bronson convinced them through letters that expressed her devotion to music and the venue. Michele had been a regular since the 1990s, where she worked in biotech startups by day and went to shows at night. After deciding to leave startups, the opportunity arose to become a venue owner. The venue will reopen under her ownership in 2027. S

Michele says to SF Gate, ““It’s an independent venue,” [...] “So many things are owned by big evil conglomerates now that really don’t think about the musicians — that take cuts of merch, that control where they can play, who they can play with. And that’s just not the ethos of Bottom of the Hill.””

name: Blondie's Bar
description: Blondie’s Bar has changed little since its opening. Named after Nicole “Blondie” DeWald, the bar was bought by Nicole’s mother and named after her. Live shows range from bluegrass, swing, latin, and jazz shows, and Blondie’s is the primary host of Valencia LIVE Street Party which features local artists.

name: Kilowatt
description: Kilowatt has evolved from a historic firehouse to a punk music venue to a sports bar and back to a live music venue. The building was constructed in 1900 as a firehouse, before becoming various independent venues in the 1980s. Notably it was a famous queer punk dance club called Paula’s Clubhouse. In 1994, electrician Peter Athanas bought the venue and named it Kilowatt, where it housed the first four annual Noise Pop Festivals. In the late 1990s, the venue’s stage was converted into a dart and pool area, turning the venue into a neighborhood sports bar. In 2022, the Kilowatt went up for sale and was purchased by local bartenders from local venues Bottom of the Hill and Thee Parkside. Bottom of the Hill was announced recently to be closing, before it was saved by a new seller, and Thee Parkside also recently closed. The new owners pushed to bring music back to the space, and started an online petition with over 2,700 supporters. The petition said, “We want to bring live music back to this legendary stage. Independent music venues took a major hit during the pandemic. Without these small humble stages - we lose the soul that made San Francisco an iconic city.” In 2022, they were able to get a Place of Entertainment Permit from the SF Entertainment Commission, allowing the Kilowatt to once again host bands, drag shows, comedy, and more. Co-owner Rick Eusey said of the decision, “I can't think of a time where I’ve seen a venue that has stopped doing music, and there’s the ability to bring that back,” he said. “It’s a really rare and incredible opportunity.”
timeline: closed in 2022 when original owner sold it, taken over under new ownership who are reviving the music

name: Biscuits and Blues
description: Biscuits and Blues quickly became a premier blues venue after its 1995 opening, hosting live local blues, soul, and R&B acts. The club closed in 2019 after a plumbing leak from an upstairs restaurant, and legal battles over the restoration throughout the pandemic kept the club closed until 2024. Extensive renovations included a new sound system. It is one of the last surviving blues focused clubs.

name: Amoeba Music
description: Amoeba Music is the world’s largest independent record store chain, originally opening in Berkeley, California in 1990. The second store opened in San Francisco, in Haight-Ashbury in 1997. The 24,000 ft store housed in a former bowling alley is packed with CDs, vinyl, records, and cassettes. The store frequently hosts musician Q&As, performances, and signings.

name: Boom Boom Room
description: Boom Boom Boom might be in the shadow of the Fillmore across the street, but it’s a home of blues and soul music in San Francisco. The club was originally opened in 1933 as Jack’s Tavern at a different location; when it moved to Fillmore Street in 1988 it was renamed. The venue was created to revive the former Fillmore neighborhood’s roots in Black jazz music, and Blues icon John Lee Hooker was a frequent visitor to the club. Notable performers include Elvis Costello, Van Morrison and David Bowie. Boom Boom Room currently hosts live music six nights a week.

name: Make-Out Room
description:
For 30 years, Make Out Room’s silver streamers, disco balls, red booths, and candle-lit bar have been the home of live music, comedy, literary events, and comedy alongside being a neighborhood bar. Early career shows have included Norah Jones, Death Cab for Cutie, Tracy Chapman, and the Decemberists. Beyond music, the bar also hosts literary events. Writers with Drinks, a monthly spoken word show, has been running since 2003 at Make Out Room. Host Charlie Jane Anders was looking for a venue that was not serious, like most would expect from a literary event, and instead had “A great sound system and the feeling of being in a nightclub.” She called The Make Out Room, “perfect” and “the best venue for something that was a little odd and kind of weird and challenging.” [...] ““San Francisco really needs to hold on to that part of its identity, that kind of feeling of being a place for artists and weirdos and people creating interesting culture,” 

In mid 2026, original owner Marty Rapalski announced that the Make Out Room, and the nearby Latin American Club would be put up for sale so he can retire. Rapalski told Mission Local , ““It’s a younger person’s game,” [...] “It needs some fresh blood and new eyes. It’s time.” Make Out Room is for sale for $450,000, and Rapalski hopes to find someone who will continue it as Make Out Room with the same heart and dedication to music and community, but he is open to any buyer. He says the worst thing would be if, “somebody came in and made it some sterile yuppie place.” The new buyer is yet to be seen.
timeline: Previously called Transfer Club during 70s, purchased by Rapalski in 1997 and reopened as Make Out Room, For Sale 2026
notes:
“Finding a venue where the owner will let you just run a regular show there for years and not worry about whether you’re making enough money for us?” Green said. “That they just trusted the artists to do something interesting is so invaluable.”

“San Francisco really needs to hold on to that part of its identity, that kind of feeling of being a place for artists and weirdos and people creating interesting culture,” Anders said.

name: Roccapulco
description: Before it was Roccapulco, the site was the home of Cesar’s Latin Palace, a prominent salsa club hosting Celia Cruz, Héctor Lavoe, Willie Colón, Eddie Palmieri, and Ray Barretto. Cesar’s Latin Palace was shut down in 1991 after being sold. It later reopened as Roccapulco where it maintains its roots as a latin night club.

name: Bird & Beckett Books & Records
typeDetails: book and record store with live music sometimes
description: Bird & Beckett is a neighborhood bookstore that accidentally became a community jazz venue. After opening in 1999, the owners met jazz musicians who started playing shows in the bookstore with the bookcases pushed aside. In 2002, they started doing weekly jazz nights every Friday called “Jazz in the Bookshop” with local performers. After fundraising to buy their own piano, and moving the entire book collection in the rain with the help of neighbors when the store changed locations, the jazz continues to this day.

name: Oracle Park
description: Oracle Park has been the home of the San Francisco Major League Baseball Giants team since 2000. Sitting right on the bay, the baseball stadium has stunning views of the water and the nearby harbor. In addition to baseball games, the park hosts large concerts with notable performers including Lady Gaga, Metallica, Ed Sheeran, and Shakira.

name: Yerba Buena Gardens Festival
description: Yerba Buena Gardens Festival is a nonprofit organization hosting free outdoor arts events from May to November in the Yerba Buena Gardens. The Yerba Buena Gardens, is a two-block park, art gallery, community center, and cultural complex on top of the Moscone Convention Center. It was created in response to activists after the urban renewal displacement of low-income, immigrant families in the area in the 70s and 80s, and mandated to guarantee free public spaces and community events. The Yerba Buena Gardens Festival hosts over 100 free outdoor concerts each year ranging from cultural celebrations to salsa nights to local bands.

name: Hardly Strictly Bluegrass
description: Hardly Strictly Bluegrass is an annual free music festival hosting more than 80 artists in Golden Gate Park. It was started by banjo player and investor Warren Hellman in 2001 as a “a gift to the people of San Francisco.” Originally named Strictly Bluegrass when it launched, the festival was later renamed to Hardly Strictly Bluegrass as its reach expanded. Founded in 2001 as "Strictly Bluegrass" by venture capitalist and banjo player Warren Hellman as a gift to the city of San Francisco. Today over half a million people attend the three-day festival.

name: The Riptide
description: The Riptide is the newest iteration of a series of bars that have lived at 3639 Taraval St. along the ocean. In 1941, the bar was “surrounded by nothing but empty streets and sand dunes from the ocean to about 19th Avenue,” wrote San Francisco Chronicle columnist Carl Nolte.” The building also is surrounded by ghost stories of drugs, murder, and ghosts. The venue became the Riptide under new ownership in 2002. David Quinby and Les James, long time patrons, bought the bar when it went up for sale because they were drawn to the music they had seen there. A fire in 2015, destroyed everything in the bar, forcing them to start over with $600,000 in damages. They reopened just over a year after the fire, and then got hit by the pandemic just as they were getting back on their feet. Today the Riptide hosts DJs, dance parties, and live bands. It’s also statistically the foggiest bar in San Francisco due to its ocean proximity.
timeline: originally opened as tavern in 1941, current owners took over in 2002, fire damaged it in 2015, reopned 2016

name: Bender's Bar and Grill
description: Bender’s Bar and Grill is a dive bar and grill in the Mission District. It has the classic pool tables, pinball, and juke box, but it’s also a love letter to San Francisco with old local signs plastering the walls. “The walls of Bender’s are somewhere between a graveyard and a hall of fame. Covered in the signs of dearly departed San Francisco businesses, walking into the bar almost feels like a shrine to a city fading into the rearview mirror.” Shortly after its opening, the bar was firebombed by an arsonist, but it was reopened a year and half later. ““We’ve been burned down once. We’ve been shuttered twice [because of COVID lockdowns]. And we’re still here.” Johnny [co-owner Johnny Davis] then sighs, “We survived COVID, we made it this far, but things have been nothing but difficult.””
timeline: temporarily closed due to an arson fire in 2006, the crew rebuilt and reopened the venue 18 months later

name: Red Poppy Art House
description: Housed in a small 650-square-foot storefront in the Mission District, the Red Poppy Art House was founded as an intercultural and multidisciplinary art and community space. It hosts artist studios, classes, jazz nights, dance performances, and exhibitions. In 2007, it joined the Intersection for the Arts to gain sponsorship before becoming an independent non profit organization in 2025. The Poppy describes itself as  “a space of multiplicity, not defined by a singular culture or aesthetic, but as a well-spring of socially engaged art and discourse that invites growth and transformation.” They host everything from Balkan funk to Middle Eastern music to Indian raga and Spanish flamenco.

name: Rickshaw Stop
description:
Named a “staple mid-size venue in San Francisco” by KQED in 2019, Rickshaw Stop has hosted several breakout artists early in their careers over their 20+ year run. The venue was cofounded in 2003 by Christopher White and Waldo Williams who wanted to start a “a party place.” Prominent music journalist Dan Strachota became the talent booker in 2004 and proceeded to book prominent early career touring acts including Billie Eilish, Sam Smith, Charli XCX, Vampire Weekend, Steve Aoki, and Phantogram to name a few. Rickshaw Stop has had excellent luck with booking such as getting Ellie Goulding in April 2014, just two weeks before she sang “Your Song” at the royal wedding for William and Kate’s first dance, and Sam Smith in 2014, right before flying to New York to do “Saturday Night Live.” 

Beyond the names though, the venue hosts weird events like a “pants off dance party” and a show powered entirely by audience members pedaling a stationary bike. White plans to run the venue “Until it’s not fun anymore.”

name: Swig Bar
owner: FutureBars, a hospitality group founded by Doug Dalton and Brian Sheehy
description: Swig Bar is a casual, no-frills cocktail Bar in Union Square. The venue hosts a weekly Sunday Night Blues Jam hosted by Adam Fumarola alongside rotating local artists, jazz ensembles, and cover bands.

name: The Independent
owner: Allen Scott (who is also the head of concerts and festivals for Another Planet Entertainment), alongside the founding group that originally opened the space in February 2004
description: One of the most notable smaller venues in San Francisco, The Independent has hosted live music for decades. It was reopened as The Independent in 2004, under management by Another Planet Entertainment. The venue hosted many breakout acts while they were first starting out like LCD Soundsystem, Bon Iver, Vampire Weekend, Zedd, and more. Major acts like Green Day, The Black Eyed Peas, John Legend, and Arctic Monkeys have also performed there. Rostam Batmangli of Vampire Weekend said, “The Independent was a venue where we could connect with each person who came to see us. We played there a few times as we were coming up and each time that connection grew stronger.”

name: Underground SF
description: Underground SF is a coffee shop during the day and transforms into an electronic music venue and nightclub by night. The venue hosts local and international DJ’s playing techno and house music alongside themed parties.

name: The Knockout
description: One of the only San Francisco bar’s that a motorcycle has ever driven through, The Knockout is central to the city’s punk scene and rebellious energy. Co-owner John Segura said of the stunt, ““I think me and Fred [co-owner Fred Schrunk] probably like that element of danger a little bit when it comes to art and music,” adds co-owner John Segura, who first opened the Knockout in 2005.” The bar aimed to fill a gap amongst local venues like El Rio by creating “a space that wasn’t dedicated to a particular scene, but to the creation of punk-influenced art in all its forms.” The SFGate adds, “The Knockout’s events calendar is one of the most diverse in the city, often featuring two events a night, and it has managed to ride the waves of taste (and weather a pandemic) for nearly 20 years.”

name: Sheba Piano Lounge
owner: sisters Netsanet (Net) Alemayehu and Israel Alemayehu
description: Sheba Piano Lounge came out of two sisters’ dream to combine their Ethiopian culture with the musical jazz history of the Fillmore neighborhood. Sheba plays music seven nights a week with no cover charge and no drink minimum, serving Ethiopian cuisine alongside specialty cocktails. The venue was designed as a restaurant and lounge first and foremost, rather than a performance venue. Regular Trisha Clayton says “It’s like being in a friends’ home—if your friend is a musician.”

name: Temple Nightclub
description:
At one point the highest grossing nightclub in SF, Temple Nightclub is known for its state of the art visual and audio systems. It features a custom DJ booth, state of the art sound system, and 50,000 LED bulb lighting installation. It also claims to have the first energy-generating dance floor in the United States, with owner Paul Hemming hoping to have all of his venues not rely on electric grids. Temple’s location also makes it a prime spot for tech entrepreneurs. 

In April 2024, Temple announced that it would close on May 25 due to financial difficulties, filing a notice that indicated 86 employees would be laid off. Despite the announcement though, the venue ultimately stayed open after internally restructuring and laying off employees.

name: Thrillhouse Records
owner: Fred Schrunk, volunteer run, non profit music store
description: Thrillhouse Records is a volunteer-run nonprofit DIY record store, specializing in punk music. Alongside punk, they carry diverse genres including alternative, metal, classical, jazz, indie rock, soul, reggae, hip hop, and more. They focus primarily on vinyl, but also carry tapes, CDs, zines, shirts, and movies. The basement of the store is an all-ages music venue hosting independent and DIY shows with low covers.

name: The Regency Ballroom
owner: Scott L. Robertson, while the venue is leased and operated by the entertainment company AEG Worldwide through its subsidiary Goldenvoice
description: Housed inside the Regency Center, Regency Ballroom is one of three event spaces in the larger center. The Regency Ballroom opened as a concert venue in 2008 under promoter Goldenvoice, while nearby venue the Warfield Theater, was closed for renovations.
timeline: 1909 opened as Scottish Rite Temple, 1966 turned into a movie theater called Regency I, 200s turned into regency ballroom

name: Outside Lands Festival
description: Outside Lands Festival is the largest independently owned music festival in the United States, celebrating its 18th year in 2026. The festival takes place in Golden Gate Park with several stages named after local landmarks and neighborhoods including Lands End, Twin Peaks, Panhandle, Sutro, and the Presidio. Outside Lands features over 100 artists each year with about 225,000 total attendees across the three day festival. The festival also features local food vendors, art exhibits and installations, and themed areas for weed, activism, and sustainability. Over $1 billion in economic impact has been injected into the city by Outside Lands since its founding in 2008.

name: Madrone Art Bar
description: Part art gallery, part dance club, Madrone Art Bar is an eclectic space featuring art works, drinks dancing, and live music. The bar was taken over from its previous owner by local artist and bartender Spike Krouse as a way to combine his two interests. Krouse has prioritized booking midweek funk and jazz bands to honor the now-gentrified neighborhood’s Black jazz history. The venue has made its mark with Krouse describing $100 tips he got during the pandemic because people cared to see it stay alive. He says, ““Having a business that's been here for so long, people have memories of what it means to them. That's what made me realize how much the place means to people. Besides it being my business, it’s theirs too.”

name: Mercury Cafe
description: Mercury Cafe is primarily a neighborhood coffee and sandwich shop with locally sourced ingredients, but it also hosts live music including Thursday night jazz and local bands on the weekends.

name: Public Works
description: Dedicated to “giving the people what they want,” Public Works hosts a diverse array of music from DJs, to underground artists, to rising talent, to comedy shows, to art exhibits. They boast a Funktion-One sound system and a springed dance floor. They offer a membership program where attendees can get access to exclusive events and discounts.

name: Royal Cuckoo Organ Lounge
owner: Paul Miller and his life and business partner, Debbie Horn
description: Widely recognized as the only organ lounge in Northern California, Royal Cuckoo Organ Lounge plays organ music five nights a week. The bar has a vintage Hammond organ built into it inspired by jazz clubs of the ‘50s and ‘60s that had organs. They only play organ music—jazz, blues, and soul—and they won’t play anything released after 1975. On Mondays and Tuesdays, vintage records are played instead.

name: Comstock Saloon
description: Featuring an original 1890s mahogany bar from when the building first opened, Comstock Saloon is a historic bar with nightly live jazz music. Since its opening in 1907, the space has hosted various bars before Comstock’s opening in 2010. The Saloon is also a museum, documenting the history of the space and its artifacts and the nightlife scene of San Francisco.

name: Brick and Mortar
owner: Michael O'Connor, Barry Smyth, and Michael Rosen
description: Brick and Mortar is a diverse music hall booking indie rock, electronic, hip hop, soul, and underground music. The venue was founded by Michael O’Connor, co-owner of The Independent, and Bruce Hansen, former owner of Coda, the supper club that was in the building before. Today Brick and Mortar hosts over 300 events annually.

name: The Lucky Horseshoe
description: A classic neighborhood dive and music bar in Bernal Heights, The Lucky Horseshoe is known for its laid back vibes and frequent live performances. It hosts a weekly Sunday Bluegrass jam, Friday Karaoke, and rotating jazz and blues nights.

name: Tupelo
description: Tupelo is a soul-food restaurant and bar with nightly live bands playing blues, jazz, funk, R&B, and zydeco music. They serve southern comfort food, cajun, and creole classics.

name: Center for New Music
owner: nonprofit, cofounded by Adam Fong and Brent Miller
description: The Center for New Music is an educational, community music space that supports local musicians with resources, rehearsal space, performance opportunities, and collaborators. The Center was created by composer-performers Adam Fong and Brent Miller who are artists and music administrators in the Bay Area and wanted to address community needs. By day the Center is a rehearsal and working space, and at night it hosts workshops and concerts. The Center for New Music is a non-profit organization.

name: Local Edition
description: EXTRA! EXTRA! READ ALL ABOUT IT! Local Edition is an underground speakeasy beneath Market Street, inspired by San Francisco’s 1950s and 60s newspaper industry. The venue sits in the former printing room of the San Francisco Examiner, in the Historic Hearst Building. It’s decorated with typewriters, clippings from old SF newspapers, and vintage paper presses. William Randolph Hearst was the founder of Hearst Corporation’s publishing and digital empire; his grandson Steve Hearst is involved with the venue and donated items from Hearst’s historical archives to decorate it with. Nightly jazz and scheduled performances bring the room to life.

name: The Chapel
description: Inside a former chapel, with 40-ft arched ceilings, The Chapel is a live music venue and bar in the Mission District. The unique building architecture creates an intimate space with strong acoustics for local and touring acts alike.

name: The Royale
description: The Royale sits inside a 106 year old historic building in Nob Hill, where it hosts free live music every weekend. Shows span jazz, funk, acoustic, underground rock, and DJ sets.

name: Feinstein's at the Nikko
description: Feinstein’s at the Nikko is a cabaret and live music venue in the lobby of the Hotel Nikko founded by Emmy and Grammy nominated performer Michael Feinstein. Performers include Tony and Grammy Award-winning artists, Broadway stars, and local acts; shows span from cabarets, live jazz sets, musical theater, comedy, drag, and pop concerts.

name: Neck of the Woods
description: In the site of the former Last Day Saloon, Neck of the Woods opened in 2013 under new management to preserve live music in the Inner Richmond. Last Day Saloon was open for nearly 40 years before closing in 2011. In 2011, the space briefly reopened as the Rocket Room before rebranding to Neck of the Woods in 2013. The venue today has a 350 capacity upstairs dance floor and a 150 capacity stage downstairs. Manager and booker Danny Berliner says that he pushes for local artists but struggles to cover expenses. “Fewer people are going out since the pandemic. They are drinking less, expenses are up and ticket prices need to remain accessible” [...] there is little or no “support system for venues to host local artists or anything like that in San Francisco.”
timeline: originally opened as Last Day Saloon, closed in 2011, reopened in 2013 as Neck of the Woods

name: SF Jazz Center
description: The “first free-standing building in America specifically built for jazz performance and education” is the SF Jazz Center in Hayes Valley. Home to SFJAZZ, a nonprofit focused on jazz education, the center hosts over 400 performances annually. The center has multiple performance spaces: the Robert N. Miner auditorium is the largest with a capacity from 350 to 700 seats and the Joe Henderson lab hosts smaller concerts and classes.

name: Gray Area
description: Gray Area is a nonprofit organization that hosts festivals, concerts, exhibitions, events, workshops, and more, at the intersection of art and technology. It was born to fill a gap in venues that focus on new media and creative technology works. In 2014, Gray Area moved to the historic Grand Theater and converted it into a performance space and venue. The renovations cost $500,000, with 200k coming from Gray Area and $300k from crowd funding. The first annual Gray Area Festival was held in 2015 following the completion of the space. In 2023, the neon sign on the building was restored and the building lit up for the first time in over 30 years.
timeline: historic venue, gray area opened inside in 2014

name: Mr. Tipple's Jazz club
description: Mr. Tipples hosts jazz music every Wednesday through Saturday alongside cocktails, dim sum, dumplings, and clay pot rice. On Wednesdays and Thursdays, headliners play three sets, and on Fridays and Saturdays, two separate acts perform. Musician Martin Diller told The Examiner after a show in 2023, “”Tipple’s has become a main staple of clubs here in San Francisco,” [...] “You can rely on a good crowd of people who are listening. But then there are also a lot of people who are maybe new to jazz, and it might even be their first jazz show. It’s just got a great vibe and energy that makes it attractive to that new audience, too.”

name: Oasis
description:
Oasis is a drag nightclub and cabaret opened in 2015 by a group including drag performers D’Arcy Drollinger and Heklina. Housed in a former gay bathhouse, the venue is central to the heart of queer nightlife and drag in San Francisco and has hosted celebrities ranging from Cher to Jane Fonda to Lil Nas X. 

In July 2025, Oasis announced that it would be closing on January 1st, 2026, 11 years after its opening on January 1st, 2015. Dollinger told the SF Chronicle, “We’ve been struggling like a lot of other venues. Our margins are razor thin,” owner D’Arcy Drollinger told the Chronicle in an exclusive interview ahead of the public announcement. “I’ve had to subsidize the club every month to be able to make it through. Those resources are gone, I’ve cashed in the majority of my retirement account to keep this going.” In an attempt to save the venue, Drollinger had reorganized the club under his nonprofit, Oasis Arts, in an attempt to raise more money and create a more sustainable business model but only raised $50,000 out of a $400,000 goal. Drollinger said “I just kept thinking things would turn around. We were waiting for that miracle to happen, and it didn’t,” Drollinger said of making the decision to close. “It’s hard when we’ve already lost so many queer spaces and so many arts organizations. I hate being another casualty.” 

The news came around the same time as the loss or near-losses of other queer clubs in San Francisco prompting concerns from the community. The Lexington Club, the city’s last remaining lesbian bar at the time, closed in 2015 amid rising rents. The Stud, a major center for queer nightlife since the 1960s, lost its longtime location in 2020 before its worker-owner collective eventually reopened the club in a new space in 2024. The historic Castro Theatre, long closely associated with LGBTQ+ film and community events, underwent a major renovation and shift toward a broader live-entertainment model under new private management in 2026. 

A miracle happened just days before the final show was scheduled. On December 26th, it was announced that venture capitalist, Mark Stevens, and his wife Mary Stevens made a multi-million dollar donation to Oasis Arts to save the venue. After a brief closing and renovation period, Oasis reopened in July 2026.
timeline: 1982- named The Oasis, reborn as modern Oasiss in 2014

name: The Midway
description: The Midway is a 40,000 square foot creative laboratory and live music venue featuring multiple indoor and outdoor rooms and an immersive 3D audiovisual listening experience. The venue hosts daytime art galleries and a cafe; by night, it hosts electronic sets and 21+ club nights.

name: NOISE
description: NOISE is a family-owned vinyl record shop, art gallery, and live music venue featuring weekly jazz sessions hosted by co-owner and saxophonist Dan Brown. “NOISE is a representation of what I remember San Francisco in the ’60s to be,” said Brown’s mom who volunteers at the store.

name: Black Cat
description: A jazz supper club with nightly performances, Black Cat coincidentally shares the name of a famous jazz supper club that existed nearby over a century ago.
timeline: closed during pandemic and reopened in 2021

name: Ocean Ale House
owner: Miles Escobedo, Daniel Silberman, and Eric Almazan.
description: Ocean Ale House is a casual American pub that recently completed an expansion with the addition of a full-size indoor stage to accommodate regular live concerts. Owners Miles Escobedo and Daniel Silberman have a 25-year plan for the business with a larger focus on live music, performances, artist residencies, and community events. Escobedo says. “We just want everybody to know that we're going to be here forever.”

name: The Great Northern
owner: Manny Alferez (also known as DJ M3) and Micah Byrne
description: Founded in 2016 by the group behind clubs Monarch and The Pawn Shop, The Great Northern is a night club featuring diverse sounds. The space underwent a brief renovation after its opening to install a custom sound system, new lighting infrastructure, and a renovated stage that could host both DJs and bands.

name: Clarion Performing Arts Center
description: Originally opened by Clara Hsu as an instrument shop in 1982, Clarion gained worldwide popularity for its traditional Chinese instruments. In 2005, Clarion was sold to long-time employees who pivoted to focusing on Chinese music before declining sales forced the venue to close in 2016. Clara then bought back the space and turned it into the Clarion Performing Arts Center where it hosts, art, music, and community events.

name: August Hall
owner: Nate Valentine, Scott Murphy, Chad Donnelly, and Justin Roja, managed by Live Nation
description: August Hall is a concert and event space in The Tenderloin district, with a long history of theater and music. The space was originally built as a Victorian Playhouse in the 1890s before becoming a United Service Organizations club called “Stage Door” for service members in World War 2. Later it started showing films as “Stage Door Theater”, notably hosting the premiere of Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo on May 9, 1958. The venue briefly turned into the Regency III movie theater in the 1980s before becoming Ruby Skye, an EDM dance club in 1990. In 2917 it transferred ownership, and after major historical restorations the venue reopened as August Hall in 2018. August Hall currently has three rooms, a live music hall with concerts booked by Live Nation, a cocktail lounge, and a bowling alley.

name: Chase Center
description: Home of the Golden State Warriors and Golden State Valkyries, Chase Center is an indoor sports and entertainment arena with 200 annual events. The arena also hosts college basketball games and about 50 concerts each year. As one of the larger venues in San Francisco, Chase Center is a significant stop for major touring acts.

name: The New Farm
description: The New Farm is a volunteer-run, grassroots community space and urban farm hosting free concerts and art exhibits and environmental education.

name: Lion’s Den Bar and Lounge
description: Lion’s Den Bar and Lounge is a speakeasy inspired by 1940s era Chinatown supper clubs. The venue has an upstairs bar and a downstairs dance floor with live music and performances, ranging from live bands and acoustic sets to jazz and R&B. Later in the night, DJs take over turning the club into a high energy dance party.

name: Blue Heron Boathouse
description: Blue Heron Boathouse in Golden Gate Park has hosted Lakehouse Jazz since 2021, a series of waterside candlelight jazz performances featuring local musicians.

name: The Mellow
description: The Mellow is a daytime coffee shop and plant store before turning into Mellow Nights, a 21+ live music and cocktail venue on Thursdays through Saturday nights.

name: Keys Jazz Bistro
owner: Institute Executive Director Simon Rowe and tech entrepreneur Matt Mullenweg, who is the co-founder of WordPress
description:
Keys Jazz Bistro hosts dinner and live music four nights a week, with a goal of celebrating and creating community around jazz music. The venue was opened in 2022 by Simon Rowe, an educator and pianist with a doctorate of musical arts performance. Rowe said to SF Weekly in 2025, “I’ve been a jazz musician for 50 years now so Keys is the culmination of my work as a player and advocate – a producer and a champion of this beautiful art form.” 

The Bistro is unique in that the intimate setting allows for closer connection between artists and listeners. Jazz musician Adam Theis explains, ““These smaller venues allow for more experimentation, where artists can be themselves and try things and it’s not all about mass appeal and trying to get the most people in the door,” [...] “Community happens more easily in smaller places…It’s a fun place to play; it’s a fun place to listen.”

name: The Lost Church
description:
The Lost Church is a nonprofit arts organization started by Brett and Elizabeth Cline in 2011 in their living room, with the mission of facilitating small performance spaces for local musicians. The mission of Lost Church is that “small venues are the backbone of regional arts and culture” because they are more closely tied to local arts scenes, employ local artists, and take chances on emerging artists. Their goals largely are to 1) create new performance spaces: 
 “Open new neighborhood spaces for live performance. Whether it’s in the back of a restaurant, a portable mini circus tent, or signing long term leases. We need new spaces!!! Our goal is to create a network of Performance Parlors that can host and nurture local and touring artists in a way that the larger spaces never can [...] There are far more Artists who can fill a 49 seat theater, than can fill a 490 seat theater. Furthermore, there are already established business models to keep the larger spaces alive.”

2) sustain existing performance spaces

“Keep performance spaces alive by instituting simple and fresh sustainable business practices. This includes proper permitting, management and promotion. Due to the massive amount of permitting and regulation involved in running a performance space, as well as often suffering from minimal to non existent promotion budgets, the average life of a smaller performance space is less than 5 years. This is normally right about the time that they finally start building up some name recognition and visibility in the community.” 

3) support small venues that are threatened 
“Whether it’s by installing sustainable business practices, supplying legal and financial support, or helping with crisis management. Our dream is to build a strong Non Profit Arts Organization that handles the running of these spaces; the leasing, booking, and promoting… and allow local members of the community to run and curate the individual nights.”

In 2022, the Clines signed a 15-year lease at 988 Columbus Ave. in North Beach where they started hosting shows in the 100 cap space before getting the city’s approval in 2023.  Performers have since said that Lost Church can feel “three times the size, based on audience response,” and is a “shining beacon of hope that the Bay Area’s music scene still has blood in its veins.”

name: Portola Music Festival
description: Portola Music Festival is an annual, 21+ electronic dance festival at Pier 80 with over 40,000 attendees daily over the 2 day event. The first and original Portola Festival was in 1909 as the city was recovering from the 1906 earthquake, with parades, floats, and fireworks, The festival was held again in 1913 and 1948 before Goldenvoice revived the name for its festival.

name: Arcana
